prs.cluster_pick_reason: 3243 changes context.lock's type from anyio.Lock to anyio.Semaphore(1, max_value=1) with an explicit rationale: httpx can resume or close the auth-flow generator from a different task than the one that acquired the lock, and anyio.Lock enforces task-affinity (raises if released by a different task under the trio backend). 2858 and 3252 both narrow or relocate where the lock is held but keep the same anyio.Lock type, so they remain exposed to that task-affinity failure mode. 3243 also adds a second flow_lock for single-flight refresh/authorization transitions, covering the same contention fix that 2858's added refresh_lock and 3252's yield-outside-lock restructuring each address separately, in one change.

clusters.pick_reason: 3243 changes context.lock's type from anyio.Lock to anyio.Semaphore(1, max_value=1) with an explicit rationale: httpx can resume or close the auth-flow generator from a different task than the one that acquired the lock, and anyio.Lock enforces task-affinity (raises if released by a different task under the trio backend). 2858 and 3252 both narrow or relocate where the lock is held but keep the same anyio.Lock type, so they remain exposed to that task-affinity failure mode. 3243 also adds a second flow_lock for single-flight refresh/authorization transitions, covering the same contention fix that 2858's added refresh_lock and 3252's yield-outside-lock restructuring each address separately, in one change.

members.title: fix(oauth): narrow context.lock scope in async_auth_flow (rebase of #2660 by @peisuke, closes #2847)
members.author: Bartok9
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #3243: context.lock is held for the entire duration of the yielded HTTP request/response in async_auth_flow, so a single long-running request (e.g. an SSE long-poll) blocks every other concurrent request going through the same OAuthClientProvider. All three PRs restructure locking in async_auth_flow to release/narrow the lock around the yield point.

clusters.pick_reason: Same fix as #3063 (reject in-flight duplicate ids) but closes two edge cases #3063 leaves open: it routes through a new `_request_stream_key()` helper that preserves int vs. string id type (str(request_id) in #3063 would collapse JSON-RPC id `1` and `"1"` into the same key, causing false-positive 409s or missed collisions across types), and it guarantees a JSON-RPC string id of `"_GET_stream"` can't collide with the reserved `GET_STREAM_KEY` sentinel used for the standalone GET stream. #3063's simpler `if request_id in self._request_streams` check doesn't handle either case.

members.title: fix(streamable-http): reject duplicate in-flight request ids
members.author: Sammy-Dabbas
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #3221: Concurrent requests reusing the same JSON-RPC request id both write into `_request_streams` keyed by that id, so the second request silently overwrites the first's routing slot and the two responses get cross-wired (one hangs, one gets the wrong payload). Both PRs add a check to reject a request whose id is already in flight.

clusters.pick_reason: #2555 adds an explicit __reduce__ directly on UrlElicitationRequiredError that reconstructs from the typed high-level fields (self._elicitations, self.message), exactly matching the class's real constructor signature, and ships an accompanying tests/shared/test_exceptions.py change exercising the pickle round-trip. #2478 introduces a `_restore_mcp_error` dispatch helper (with a type-based special case for UrlElicitationRequiredError) and removes the `pragma: no cover` on MCPError.data, but the diff shown does not include any `__reduce__` wiring that actually calls this new helper, nor any test changes — so it's unclear from the PR's own diff that it fully closes the reported TypeError, and its dispatch-by-type approach would need updating every time a new MCPError subclass with a divergent constructor is added, whereas #2555's per-class __reduce__ is self-contained and localized to the subclass that has the incompatible signature.

clusters.pick_reason: 3243 changes context.lock's type from anyio.Lock to anyio.Semaphore(1, max_value=1) with an explicit rationale: httpx can resume or close the auth-flow generator from a different task than the one that acquired the lock, and anyio.Lock enforces task-affinity (raises if released by a different task under the trio backend). 2858 and 3252 both narrow or relocate where the lock is held but keep the same anyio.Lock type, so they remain exposed to that task-affinity failure mode. 3243 also adds a second flow_lock for single-flight refresh/authorization transitions, covering the same contention fix that 2858's added refresh_lock and 3252's yield-outside-lock restructuring each address separately, in one change.

members.title: fix(oauth): narrow context.lock scope in async_auth_flow (rebase of #2660 by @peisuke, closes #2847)
members.author: Bartok9
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #3243: context.lock is held for the entire duration of the yielded HTTP request/response in async_auth_flow, so a single long-running request (e.g. an SSE long-poll) blocks every other concurrent request going through the same OAuthClientProvider. All three PRs restructure locking in async_auth_flow to release/narrow the lock around the yield point.

clusters.pick_reason: Same fix as #3063 (reject in-flight duplicate ids) but closes two edge cases #3063 leaves open: it routes through a new `_request_stream_key()` helper that preserves int vs. string id type (str(request_id) in #3063 would collapse JSON-RPC id `1` and `"1"` into the same key, causing false-positive 409s or missed collisions across types), and it guarantees a JSON-RPC string id of `"_GET_stream"` can't collide with the reserved `GET_STREAM_KEY` sentinel used for the standalone GET stream. #3063's simpler `if request_id in self._request_streams` check doesn't handle either case.

members.title: fix(streamable-http): reject duplicate in-flight request ids
members.author: Sammy-Dabbas
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #3221: Concurrent requests reusing the same JSON-RPC request id both write into `_request_streams` keyed by that id, so the second request silently overwrites the first's routing slot and the two responses get cross-wired (one hangs, one gets the wrong payload). Both PRs add a check to reject a request whose id is already in flight.
